text:
The passages describe three relevant approaches:

- **Assistance games:** Explicitly distinguish information about **how the world works** from information about **what people value**, and represent the limited amount of value information humans can provide. The proposed mechanism is to constrain or “regularize” the AI’s behavior—including how quickly it changes the world—according to how much it actually knows about human goals, rather than assuming humans have specified what to do in every unfamiliar situation. (https://www.alignmentforum.org/posts/fzFyCJ6gB9kBL9RqW/axrp-episode-8-assistance-games-with-dylan-hadfield-menell)

- **Anomaly detection with fail-safes:** Detect unusual behavior or novel failure modes before the system enters a more hazardous state, and trigger a fail-safe when it encounters unfamiliar, highly uncertain situations. This reduces exposure to hazards and provides an additional layer of protection alongside other safety measures. (https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.05862)

- **Broader moral-judgment data and bias reduction:** Delphi uses diverse, situation-specific human ethical judgments and incorporates Social Bias Frames to try to reduce demographic biases. (https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.07574) Its authors also propose collecting judgments interactively from the wider public, including adversarial examples, to capture broader opinions than narrowly representative crowdsourced annotations; however, they report that cultural, temporal, and demographic reliability problems remain unresolved. (https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.07574)
